title: The small fossil
prompt: This fossil cast has a tiny feature that changes how it is understood. You have time to open one part of the display. Which would you choose?
intro: It’s a very small fossil, but the label has rather a lot to say. Which part would you open?

choices.text: How the curators worked out what kind of animal it was.
choices.evidence: Chose the evidence behind the fossil’s identification.

choices.text: Which parts are original fossil, and which were restored.
choices.evidence: Wanted to distinguish surviving material from later restoration.

choices.text: A chance to study it without the label, then reveal the explanation.
choices.evidence: Chose space for a first-hand impression before reading the answer.

choices.text: What different visitors noticed when they first saw it.
choices.evidence: Wanted several perspectives on the same fossil.

title: The missing piece
prompt: This skeleton is missing one piece. Which version would you rather encounter in the museum?
intro: There’s a gap just there. We know something belonged in it, but not quite what.

choices.text: Show two possible reconstructions beside the gap so I can compare them.
choices.evidence: Preferred competing explanations to a single reconstruction.

choices.text: Leave the gap visible so I can see exactly what remains.
choices.evidence: Kept an absence visible rather than filling it in.

choices.text: Add a clearly marked, removable replica so I can picture the whole animal.
choices.evidence: Chose a reversible way to move forward with incomplete information.

choices.text: Let visitors switch between the possible versions themselves.
choices.evidence: Made room for different ways of understanding the skeleton.

title: A trace of an ordinary day
prompt: This trace-fossil wall has one empty archive slot. If you added a small record of an ordinary day, what would you put at its centre?
intro: Most days don’t leave fossils. We could keep one small trace of yours, though.

choices.text: An unanswered question I kept returning to.
choices.evidence: Kept an unresolved question as the day’s central record.

choices.text: A small routine I might otherwise forget.
choices.evidence: Preserved an easily overlooked part of everyday life.

choices.text: A decision that changed how the day went.
choices.evidence: Focused on a moment of making a difference.

choices.text: An exchange with someone that stayed with me.
choices.evidence: Remembered the day through an interaction.

title: The surprise drawer
prompt: A mineral drawer opens to two trays: one familiar sample and one unexpected find. You only have time for one arrangement. What is closest to your instinct?
intro: The second tray wasn’t on my list. It does look interesting, doesn’t it?

choices.text: Read a little more about both samples before choosing which to examine.
choices.evidence: Sought more context before choosing.

choices.text: Stay with the familiar sample and give it the closer look I planned.
choices.evidence: Protected an existing intention while leaving a future opening.

choices.text: Switch to the unexpected sample; I can return to the familiar one later.
choices.evidence: Accepted an opportunity while treating the original plan as recoverable.

choices.text: Place both trays side by side and compare them with someone.
choices.evidence: Looked for a shared comparison that kept both options in view.

title: The next test
prompt: If you were helping the museum choose one next step for this unfamiliar meteorite, which would you back?
intro: One meteorite, one bit of funding, and four sensible forms. I’m glad it isn’t my decision.

choices.text: A detailed scan: more information, though it may not settle the main question.
choices.evidence: Accepted an incomplete answer in exchange for more evidence.

choices.text: Better storage first: protect the meteorite, though the answer will wait.
choices.evidence: Protected future options before pursuing an immediate answer.

choices.text: A tiny sample test: a clearer answer, but it permanently uses some material.
choices.evidence: Accepted a stated cost for a more decisive next step.

choices.text: A joint study with another museum: shared expertise, but a slower start.
choices.evidence: Chose shared expertise despite a coordination cost.

title: Same samples, different view
prompt: You and another visitor study the same two mineral samples but leave very different notes. What would you want to do next?
intro: Same samples, two different labels. Neither one looks obviously wrong to me.

choices.text: Compare the particular details each of us noticed.
choices.evidence: Explored the observations behind different impressions.

choices.text: Keep both accounts intact; neither needs replacing yet.
choices.evidence: Preserved separate accounts without forcing resolution.

choices.text: Try a different viewing angle together and see what changes.
choices.evidence: Used another experience to move beyond the disagreement.

choices.text: Ask why that impression of the samples mattered to them.
choices.evidence: Prioritised the personal significance of another perspective.

title: Room to change
prompt: This miniature habitat is being redesigned. The proposal has real benefits, but it will feel different. What would you speak up for first?
intro: Here’s the old habitat, and here’s the proposal. They moved nearly everything.

choices.text: A clear account of what the habitat change is meant to improve.
choices.evidence: Asked for the purpose and evidence behind a change.

choices.text: Keep one feature that makes the habitat feel like itself.
choices.evidence: Protected a specific source of continuity.

choices.text: Use a trial layout before making the redesign permanent.
choices.evidence: Favoured a practical, reversible trial.

choices.text: Let the keepers and regular visitors help shape the proposal.
choices.evidence: Prioritised participation by the people affected.

title: The shared field kit
prompt: A small group is taking this field kit somewhere unfamiliar. The basics are packed, with room for one extra item. What would you add?
intro: The sensible things are packed. There’s just enough room for one interesting thing.

choices.text: A field guide, so we can make sense of what we find.
choices.evidence: Brought a resource for interpreting discoveries together.

choices.text: A notebook, so details don’t disappear when the day ends.
choices.evidence: Made room to retain details beyond the moment.

choices.text: A map with a few optional detours marked.
choices.evidence: Kept room for self-directed exploration within a usable plan.

choices.text: A shared camera, so everyone can add what caught their eye.
choices.evidence: Chose a shared record that others could shape.
